title: Comet McNaught over the Atacama Desert
caption: Comet McNaught over the Atacama Desert, near Antofagasta, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile

recognition.text: Published in the ESO image archive. No published rating.

story: Comet C/2006 P1, better known as Comet McNaught, is seen here from the coast of Chile's II Region, near Antofagasta. The comet reached perihelion, its closest point to the Sun, in January 2007, and unexpectedly became the brightest comet in the previous 40 years.

Conditions for professional astronomy in this corner of the Atacama Desert are excellent, and the II Region is home to several major facilities. ESO's Very Large Telescope stands some 120 km south of Antofagasta and is described as the world's most advanced optical-infrared observatory on the ground.

When the photo was released, ALMA, the world's largest radio observatory, was being built at 5000 metres near San Pedro de Atacama. Cerro Armazones, a mountain 3046 metres high and about 20 km from Paranal, had been chosen for the Extremely Large Telescope.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera on the Chilean coast, in visible light. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the comet's fainter outer parts may appear more extensive here than they would to someone watching.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: ESO Photo Ambassador Gerhard Hüdepohl took the photograph. Comets like McNaught are icy bodies that grow bright as they approach the Sun and release gas and dust, and this one surprised observers by how brilliant it became.
alt: A bright comet in the sky above the Atacama Desert coast near Antofagasta.
